Part A

Preparation, isolation, interconversion

From Stock's magnesium boride to controlled cage growth.

A
Part A.
Preparation · history

Stock (1912): magnesium boride and acid

B2O3 + Mg (excess) → "magnesium boride" + MgO

magnesium boride + HCl(aq) → B4H10 + other boranes + H2

B4H10 → B2H6 + higher boranes (on standing or warming)

  • Main product B4H10, in a few per cent yield; silanes also form from silicide impurity.
  • B2H6 was first obtained by heating B4H10 (1913).

Why it mattered

Stock's high-vacuum techniques turned a "green-flame gas" into a series of definite, characterised compounds: B2H6, B4H10, B5H9, B5H11, B6H10, B10H14.

A. Stock, C. Massenez, Ber. 1912, 45, 3539; A. Stock, K. Friederici, Ber. 1913, 46, 1959; Wade (1971), §4-3; course PPT slides 89 and 13.
Wade: "the hydrolysis of magnesium boride remains a practicable route to hexaborane(10), but diborane is now the material from which most of the higher hydrides are prepared."
Isolation

Isolation: trap-to-trap distillation on a vacuum line

  • The mixture diffuses through V-traps at falling temperatures; each borane condenses where it is no longer volatile.
  • Only glass and mercury touch the sample (mercury float valves, manometers); air and grease are excluded. Products are identified by vapour pressure and vapour density.
Wade (1971), §4-2, Figs. 4-5 and 4-6 (trap temperatures −78, −126, −196 °C for B5H11, B4H10, B2H6); A. Stock, Hydrides of Boron and Silicon, Cornell, 1933.
Boranes are volatile, air-sensitive (some pyrophoric) and react with grease and moisture, so Stock developed an all-glass vacuum line. The same principle is used in modern Schlenk and vacuum-line work.
Preparation · diborane

Making diborane today

routeequation
Schlesinger & Burg (1931)2 BCl3 + 5 H2 → B2H5Cl + 5 HCl;  6 B2H5Cl ⇌ 5 B2H6 + 2 BCl3 (discharge)
borohydride + BF33 NaBH4 + 4 BF3 → 2 B2H6 + 3 NaBF4 (diglyme)
LiAlH4 + BCl34 BCl3 + 3 LiAlH4 → 2 B2H6 + 3 LiCl + 3 AlCl3
NaH + BF38 BF3 + 6 NaH → B2H6 + 6 NaBF4
NaBH4 + I22 NaBH4 + I2 → B2H6 + 2 NaI + H2 (diglyme)

In practice

B2H6 is usually generated as needed, or replaced by the adducts H3B·THF and H3B·SMe2, which are safer to store.

Das, §10.12.7(a)–(b); H. I. Schlesinger, A. B. Burg, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1931, 53, 4321; NaBH4/BF3 and NaBH4/I2: standard laboratory routes (recalled; equations balanced here).
Ask the class to check the balancing of each equation.
Preparation · higher boranes

Heating diborane gives the higher boranes

Mild conditions give arachno B4H10 and B5H11; hotter conditions (with H2) give the more stable nido B5H9 and B10H14.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F–O, pp. 255–265; Stone, Q. Rev. 1955; Das, §10.12.7(c).
Products are separated by trap-to-trap distillation (previous slide).
Preparation · mechanism

Cages grow by gaining BH3 and losing H2

  • B2H6 ⇌ 2 BH3: reactive BH3 is the building block.
  • BH3 + B2H6 → B3H9 → B3H7 + H2.
  • B3H7 + BH3 → B4H10;  B3H7 + B2H6 → B5H11 + H2.
  • B2H6 + 2 B4H10 ⇌ 2 B5H11 + 2 H2.
Das, §10.12.7(c); Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F–H (Schaeffer's B3H7 intermediate; Schlesinger equilibrium).
A simplified mechanism, but it captures the logic of BH3 addition and H2 loss.
Interconversion

Interconverting the boranes

reactionconditionstype
5 B4H10 → 2 B5H9 + 5 B2H6 + H2B3H7·L catalysisarachno → nido
2 B5H11 → B6H10 + 2 B2H6weak base (Me2O)arachno → larger nido
2 B5H9 → B10H16 + H2electric dischargejoining cages
B9H15 → B5H9 + …Me2Odegradation
B10H14 + 2 R3N → [R3NH]2[B10H10]heatnido → closo
6 B2H6 + 2 R3N → [R3NH]2[B12H12] + 11 H2≈ 150 °Cbuilding a closo cage
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F, G, I, P and §5.6, pp. 255–289; Das, §10.12.7(e).
Balance check for the first: 5 B4H10 = B20H50; 2 B5H9 + 5 B2H6 + H2 = B20H(18+30+2) = B20H50.
Interconversion · one boron at a time

Remove H⁺, insert BH3, add H⁺

  • A bridging H is acidic; KH removes it, leaving an electron-rich B–B bond.
  • That B–B bond picks up BH3 (from ½ B2H6); HCl then releases the larger borane.

B5H9 + KH → K[B5H8] + H2
K[B5H8] + ½ B2H6 → K[B6H11]
K[B6H11] + HCl → B6H10 + H2 + KCl

Das, §10.12.7(d); method of S. G. Shore and co-workers (1970s), see Greenwood & Earnshaw, 2nd edn, §6.7.3.
The same sequence takes B4H10 to B5H11.

Individual boranes · arachno

Tetraborane(10), B4H10: the butterfly

B4H10, 4 bridges (teal)
drag to rotate
  • Two hinge BH and two wing-tip BH2; four B–H–B bridges along the wing edges.
  • Bridges are unsymmetrical: the long B···H (1.43 Å) goes to the BH2 boron.
  • m.p. −120 °C, b.p. 16.1 °C; decomposes at room temperature.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5F, pp. 231, 255; structure: C. E. Nordman, W. N. Lipscomb, J. Chem. Phys. 1953, 21, 1856.
Stock's first characterised borane (1912).
Individual boranes · nido

Pentaborane(9), B5H9: the square pyramid

B5H9, C4v
drag to rotate
  • Apical BH over a square of four BH; four bridges on the basal edges.
  • b.p. 58.4 °C, m.p. −46.1 °C; thermally very stable but ignites in air.
  • Made by pyrolysis of B2H6 with H2 at ≈ 250 °C.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5G, pp. 258–259; structure: W. J. Dulmage, W. N. Lipscomb, Acta Cryst. 1952, 5, 260.
Studied as a high-energy fuel in the 1950s.

drag to rotate

arachno-B5H11 · 3 bridges

b.p. 63 °C; first product of B2H6 pyrolysis

B–B 1.60 Å (unbridged edge); b.p. 108 °C

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5H–I, pp. 262–264; structures: L. R. Lavine, W. N. Lipscomb, J. Chem. Phys. 1954, 22, 614; F. L. Hirshfeld et al., J. Chem. Phys. 1958, 28, 56.
In B6H10 the four bridges hop round the five basal edges, so all basal B look equivalent by NMR.
Individual boranes · nido

Decaborane(14), B10H14: the basket

B10H14, C2v
drag to rotate
  • Ten BH in a boat-shaped basket; four bridges on the open face (B5–B6, B6–B7, B8–B9, B9–B10).
  • White solid, m.p. 99.7 °C; the only neutral borane stable in air.
  • Made by pyrolysis of B2H6 at 100–200 °C; first borane solved by X-ray (1950).
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5O, p. 265, Fig. 5.16; J. S. Kasper, C. M. Lucht, D. Harker, Acta Cryst. 1950, 3, 436.
The most versatile borane: starting point for B10H10 2−, carboranes and much of Part D.
Individual boranes · larger

boranenotes

Hawthorne (1967), §5.2 and §5.5L–S, Fig. 5.1(g, i, k, l).
Conjuncto boranes are made by joining smaller cages: a two-centre B–B bond, a shared edge, or fusion.

General reactions · overview

Eight types of borane reaction

typewhat happensexample
1. Oxidation, solvolysisB–H → B–O; H2 releasedB5H9 + 15 H2O → 5 B(OH)3 + 12 H2
2. Halogenationterminal H replaced by XB2H6 + HBr → B2H5Br + H2
3. Lewis base cleavagebridges broken; BH3 or BH2⁺ removedB4H10 + 2 NH3 → [H2B(NH3)2][B3H8]
4. Base addition, no cleavagecage opens (nido → arachno)B10H14 + 2 MeCN → B10H12(MeCN)2 + H2
5. Deprotonationbridging H lost as H⁺B6H10 + KH → K[B6H9] + H2
6. Electrophilic substitutionH replaced at e⁻-rich BB5H9 + MeCl → 1-MeB5H8 + HCl (AlCl3)
7. Hydride/electron additionanions; cage opens or growsB10H14 + 2 Na → Na2[B10H14]
8. HydroborationB–H adds to C=CB4H10 + C2H4 → C2H4B4H8 + H2
Classification following K. F. Purcell, J. C. Kotz, Inorganic Chemistry, Saunders, 1977 (from memory; please check pages) and Das, §10.13.2; examples from Hawthorne (1967), §5.5, who reports Lipscomb's structural work.
Type 8 example: Hawthorne writes the ethylene product of B4H10 as C2H4B4H8; the H2 balances it.
Type 1 · oxidation and solvolysis

Burning and hydrolysis: every B–H gives H2

reactionnote
B2H6 + 3 O2 → B2O3 + 3 H2Overy exothermic
2 B5H9 + 12 O2 → 5 B2O3 + 9 H2Oignites in air
B2H6 + 6 H2O → 2 B(OH)3 + 6 H2fast
B4H10 + 12 H2O → 4 B(OH)3 + 11 H2Stock
B10H14 + 30 H2O → 10 B(OH)3 + 22 H2slow; needs heat
B2H6 + 6 MeOH → 2 B(OMe)3 + 6 H2alcoholysis

One rule balances them all

BnHm + 3n H2O → n B(OH)3 + ½(3n + m) H2

Hydridic Hδ− on boron meets protic Hδ+ of water.

The cage-closed B10H14 and B12H12²⁻ resist hydrolysis far better than the open, small boranes.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F (B4H10), §5.6 (B12H12²⁻); Das, §10.13.2(a)–(c); Stone (1955). The B5H9 and B10H14 equations are balanced from the general rule.
Exercise: balance B6H10 + H2O. Answer: B6H10 + 18 H2O → 6 B(OH)3 + 14 H2.
Type 2 · halogenation

Halogenation: a terminal H is replaced

reactionwhere X goes
B2H6 + HBr → B2H5Br + H2terminal; bridges survive
B5H9 + Br2 → 1-BrB5H8 + HBrapex B1
B5H9 + I2 → 1-IB5H8 + HIapex B1
B10H14 + I2 → 2-IB10H13 + HIB2 (also some 1-I)
B10H14 + 2 I2 → 2,4-I2B10H12 + 2 HIB2, B4 (X-ray)
  • For B5H9 and B10H14 this is electrophilic substitution (Type 6): X goes to the most electron-rich boron.
  • Halides couple like alkyl halides: 2 B2H5I + 2 Na → B4H10 + 2 NaI.
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5C, p. 249; §5.5G, pp. 260–261; §5.5O.6, p. 270 (2,4-I2B10H12: Schaeffer, X-ray); Schlesinger & Burg (1931).
Positions are fixed by 11B NMR (and one X-ray study for the diiodide).
Type 3 · Lewis base cleavage

Symmetric cleavage: L·BH3 is split off

B4H10 + 2 NMe3 → Me3N·B3H7 + Me3N·BH3a wing-tip BH2 leaves as BH3
B5H11 + 2 CO → H3B·CO + B4H8·COCO as the base
B6H12 + PMe3 → H3B·PMe3 + B5H9arachno → nido
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5A, C, F, H, pp. 244–263; Das, §10.13.2(d)(i).
Bulky or soft bases (Me3N, PR3, THF, Me2S, CO) give L→BH3.
Type 3 · Lewis base cleavage

Unsymmetric cleavage: [H2BL2]⁺ is split off

B4H10 + 2 NH3 → [H2B(NH3)2]⁺[B3H8]⁻Hawthorne Fig. 5.13
B6H12 + 2 NH3 → [H2B(NH3)2]⁺[B5H10]⁻Das
B4H10 + 2 Me2NH → 2 μ-Me2N-B2H5 + H2amine breaks the cage
S. G. Shore, R. W. Parry, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1958, 80, 8; Hawthorne (1967), §5.5C, F, pp. 251–258; Das, §10.13.2(d)(i).
Small, hard bases (NH3, MeNH2) attack the same boron twice. The "diammoniate of diborane" was proved ionic by Parry and Shore.
Type 3 · mechanism

Where does the second base go?

Small, hard bases attack the same boron again: [L2BH2]⁺[BH4]⁻.

Bulky or soft bases attack the other boron: 2 L·BH3.

Singly bridged intermediate: Parry and Shore, as in Hawthorne (1967), §5.5C; steric and hard–soft rationale: Das, §10.13.2(d)(i).
Step 1 is common: one base opens one bridge, giving L–BH2–H–BH3. Step 2 decides. Hawthorne notes that for B4H10 the cleavage may always be unsymmetric first, with the products set by later ligand exchange.
Type 4 · base addition without cleavage

Base addition: the cage stays whole but opens

reactionchange
B10H14 + 2 MeCN → B10H12(MeCN)2 + H2nido → arachno
B10H14 + 2 Et2S → B10H12(SEt2)2 + H2nido → arachno
B5H9 + 2 NMe3 → B5H9(NMe3)2nido → hypho (isolable)
B5H9 + Me2NCH2CH2NMe2 → B5H9·(tmeda)1 : 1 adduct

Why the cage opens

Each L brings an electron pair into the cluster: one more skeletal pair, so one more open vertex.

Then cleavage may follow

B5H9(NMe3)2 + NMe3 → B4H6(NMe3)2 + Me3N·BH3

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5G, pp. 260–262; §5.5O.8, pp. 274–277 (Schaeffer, 1957); "hypho" label: Das, §10.12.
The B10 case is drawn in Part D, where the structural change is shown with all hydrogens.
Type 5 · deprotonation

Deprotonation: a bridging H leaves as H⁺

B4H10 + KH → K[B4H9] + H2
B5H9 + KH → K[B5H8] + H2
B6H10 + KH → K[B6H9] + H2
B10H14 + OH⁻ ⇌ B10H13⁻ + H2O
B10H14 + NaH → Na[B10H13] + H2
  • Larger cages are stronger acids: B5H9 < B6H10 < B10H14 (pKa ≈ 2.7).
  • The new B–B bond is the site where BH3 inserts: the route up the series in Part A.
Das, §10.12.6(d) and §10.13.2(d)(ii); Hawthorne (1967), §5.5O.3, pp. 267–268 (Guter and Schaeffer: B10H14 titrates as a monoprotic acid).
Proof that the acidic H is a bridge H: in D2O/dioxane only the four bridge H exchange first (Hawthorne, p. 268).
Type 6 · electrophilic substitution

Electrophiles go to the most electron-rich boron

reaction (AlCl3 catalyst)site
B5H9 + RCl → 1-RB5H8 + HClapex B1
B5H9 + C2H4 → 1-EtB5H8apex B1 (alkene as R⁺ source)
B5H9 + DCl → 1-DB5H8 + HClonly the apical H exchanges
B10H14 + RBr → RB10H13 + HBrB1–B4; 2-R : 1-R ≈ 3 : 1
B10H14 + DCl → B10H13D + HClonly B1–B4 exchange

Like Friedel–Crafts

The site matches the ground-state charge: the B5H9 apex and B2/B4 of B10H14 carry the most negative charge (charge map in Part D).

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5G, pp. 260–261 and §5.5O.6, pp. 270–271 (Williams; Onak); Das, §10.13.2(d)(iii).
Hawthorne cautions that ground-state charges only roughly predict the sites; the mechanism was still open in 1967.
Type 7 · hydride and electron addition

Hydride and electron addition

B2H6 + 2 NaH → 2 NaBH4BH4⁻ (diglyme)
NaBH4 + B2H6 → NaB3H8 + H2cage grows
B10H14 + 2 Na → Na2[B10H14]nido → arachno (Part D)
B10H14 + BH4⁻ → B11H14⁻ + 2 H2 (via B10H13⁻, 90 °C)cage grows
Hawthorne (1967), §5.5A, D, pp. 244, 252–253; §5.5O.7, p. 272; §5.5Q, pp. 284–285; Das, §10.12.6.
B2H7− keeps one B–H–B bridge: half-way to two BH4−. The overall B11H14− equation is summed from Hawthorne's two steps.
Type 8 · hydroboration

Hydroboration: B–H adds across C=C

  • B adds to the less substituted carbon, H to the more substituted one, on the same face (syn).
  • H2O2/OH⁻ then gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

Higher boranes too

B4H10 + C2H4 → C2H4B4H8 + H2; B5H11 + C2H4 → EtB5H10. With AlCl3, B5H9 is substituted instead.

Das, §10.13.2(e); H. C. Brown, B. C. Subba Rao, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1956, 78, 5694; Hawthorne (1967), §5.5F, H, pp. 258, 263.
Four-centre transition state explains the syn addition.

Tetraborane(10)

Reactions · B5H9

B5H9 + I2 → 1-IB5H8 + HIelectrophile at the apex
1-RB5H8 → 2-RB5H8200 °C, or 2,6-lutidine / NMe3

Base route: a bridge H⁺ is removed, the B5H8⁻ skeleton rearranges, and R ends on a basal boron (intramolecular).

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5G, pp. 260–261, Fig. 5.15 (Onak and Gerhart; Hough, Edwards and Stang); Das, §10.13.2(d), Fig. 10.13.2.2.
The drawing is kept here because it shows where X sits before and after.

nido-B5H9

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5G and §5.5P, pp. 260–262, 283–284 (Grimes, Wang, Lewin and Lipscomb: B10H16 structure); Das, §10.12.6(d). B10H16 model built from two B5H8 units for teaching.
B10H16: each half is B5H9 minus its apical H; the two apices are joined by a two-centre B–B bond. Every other reported reaction of B10H16 gives B10H14 or a B10H12 derivative.
Reactions · B5H11, B6H10, B6H12

Pentaborane(11) and the hexaboranes

B5H11: behaves as "B4H8 + BH3"

B5H11 ⇌ B4H8 + BH3
B5H11 + 2 CO → H3B·CO + B4H8CO

B5H11 + B4H10 → B5H9 + 2 B2H6

B6H10 and B6H12

In B6H10 the four bridge H move rapidly round the five basal borons (¹¹B NMR).

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5H–J, pp. 262–264 (Burg and Spielman; Schaeffer; Gaines and Schaeffer); Das, §10.13.2(d)(i)–(ii).

Reactions · B10H14 (1)

Decaborane(14) is a Brønsted acid

B10H14 + NaH → Na[B10H13] + H2 (Et2O)B10H14 + CH3MgI → B10H13MgI + CH4
B10H14 + Ph3P=CH2 → [Ph3PCH3][B10H13]B10H13MgI + RX → 6-RB10H13 + MgXI
Topology after Lipscomb, as drawn in Hawthorne (1967), Fig. 5.18; reactions: §5.5O.3–4, pp. 267–270 (Guter and Schaeffer; Siegel; Dunstan).
Losing a bridge proton turns one B–H–B into a B–B bond (red). In D2O the four bridge H exchange first, then spread to B5–B10; B1–B4 keep their H.

A charge map predicts the sites

positioncharge / eattacked by
2, 4−0.254electrophiles

  • I2 → 2-I and 2,4-I2; RBr/AlCl3 → 2-R : 1-R ≈ 3 : 1.

Reactions · B10H14 (3)

Add two electrons: nido-B10H14 → arachno-B10H14²⁻

B10H14 + 2 Na → Na2[B10H14] (NH3(l))
B10H13⁻ + BH4⁻ → B10H14²⁻ + BH3 (H2O)
B10H14 + 2 L → B10H12L2 + H2
B10H14²⁻ + 2 pyH⁺ → B10H12py2 + 2 H2

What changed (Lipscomb)

B6 and B9 become BH2 (or BHL); the bridges move to 5–10 and 7–8. Skeletal pairs 12 → 13: nido → arachno.

Topology predicted by Lipscomb and drawn in Hawthorne (1967), Fig. 5.19; confirmed by X-ray of B10H12(MeCN)2 (Fig. 5.21); reactions §5.5O.7–8, pp. 271–277 (Toeniskoetter; Muetterties; Schaeffer).
Ligand strength (each displaces the one to its left): R2S ≈ RCN < R2NCN < R2NCOR < R3N < R3P ≈ pyridine. Hawthorne prints one H2 for B10H14 2− + 2 pyH+; two are needed to balance. B10H12L2 are best seen as substituted B10H14 2− ions: L replaces H− at B6 and B9.

Solvolysis removes the B6 or B9 boron (the one carrying BH2) as B(OR)3, leaving an arachno-B9H13L.

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5O.9–12, pp. 277–282 (Knoth and Muetterties; Graybill, Pitochelli and Hawthorne; Schaeffer, X-ray of B9H13(MeCN), Fig. 5.22).

Hawthorne (1967), §5.6A.2, pp. 288–289, Fig. 5.25 (mechanism: L dissociates, Et3N removes H⁺, B10H11⁻ → B10H10²⁻); Das, §10.12.6(e).

B11H14⁻ is an icosahedron missing one vertex; its three extra H move rapidly over the open face (Lipscomb's prediction, then found).

Hawthorne (1967), §5.5Q, pp. 284–285 (Moore, Lohr and Lipscomb; Aftandilian, Miller, Parshall and Muetterties) and §5.6A.1, p. 287; Das, §10.12.6(e).
The first equation is the 25 °C step as printed by Hawthorne (H3BOR2 is shown as giving B2H6 + R2O). Intermediates on the way to B12H12 2− include B3H8− and B11H14−.

Use for revision: deprotonation, adducts, reduction, closure, substitution.
Summary

Key points

  • Stock: magnesium boride + acid → B4H10; separated by trap-to-trap distillation (−78, −126, −196 °C).
  • B2H6 from NaBH4 + BF3 or LiAlH4 + BCl3; pyrolysis gives higher boranes; KH/BH3 adds one B at a time.
  • Reactions: solvolysis, halogenation, symmetric/unsymmetric cleavage, base addition, deprotonation, substitution, hydride addition, hydroboration.
  • B10H14 (Lipscomb topologies): acid → B10H13⁻; +2e⁻ or 2 L → arachno B10H14²⁻ / B10H12L2; Et3N → closo B10H10²⁻; BH4⁻ → B11H14⁻.
Hawthorne (1967), ch. 5; Das, §10.12–10.13; Wade (1971), ch. 4.
Ask students to draw the product of each type with all hydrogens.
Check your understanding

Questions (press → to reveal each answer)

1. Why does NH3 cleave B2H6 unsymmetrically but NMe3 symmetrically?
NH3 is small and hard and attacks the same boron twice; NMe3 is too bulky and attacks the other boron.
2. How would you separate B2H6, B4H10 and B5H11?
Trap-to-trap distillation: B5H11 at −78 °C, B4H10 at −126 °C, B2H6 at −196 °C.
3. Which B of B10H14 is attacked by I2, and which by MeCN?
I2 (electrophile): B2 and B4. MeCN (base): B6 and B9.
4. Make B6H10 from B5H9.
KH, then ½ B2H6, then HCl.
Based on these notes.
Allow a minute per question.
